newsitem.title: PERU: Peru searches for miners after quake kills 13.
newsitem.headline: Peru searches for miners after quake kills 13.

text.p: Rescue workers tried on Wednesday to reach remote mining villages in southern Peru, where several miners were feared trapped underground after an earthquake that killed at least 13 people and injured 500.
Tens of thousands of people spent the night on the streets after their houses were destroyed by the quake, which shook southern Peru at midday on Tuesday and rocked Lima for a minute.

The hardest-hit towns were along the Pacific coast: Nazca, 290 miles (460 km) to the south of the capital Lima, where 300 were injured and Ica, 100 miles (160 km) further north, where another 200 were injured, officials said on Wednesday.
Army and police flew tents, blankets and food supplies into Nazca, where six of the deaths occurred. The quake left over 5,000 homes uninhabitable, the Civil Defence said.

Fire Chief Otacar Lucar, coordinating rescue operations from Nazca, said there were reports that 13 miners were trapped in three gold mining zones in the departament of Ica at Incas, Salamarca, Ingenio.
"I ran out of the mine but my two friends ... were trapped in there," Julian Huaman, who walked 14 miles (23 km) to Nazca after escaping from the collapsing mine, told Reuters.

One miner died in Moyohauca, 375 miles (600 km) south of Lima, in the department of Arequipa and 10 more were seriously injured, said Celso Cahachahua, a community leader in the mining village, without giving more details.

A Civil Defence official, Pedro Rivera, said rescue workers at the site confirmed no miners were trapped in the Huanca gold mine, 310 miles (500 km) to the south of Lima, where earlier 300 miners were feared stuck underground.
The quake measured 6.4 on the Richter scale and its epicentre was 65 miles (100 km) southeast of Ica, according to Luis Vilca of the Peruvian Geophysic Institute.
By early on Wednesday, Nazca had experienced at least 200 aftershocks, including one late Tuesday that measured 4.2 on the Richter scale, Vilca said.

Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi, the top government official in the absence of President Alberto Fujimori, who was on a tour of Japan and Southeast Asia, said he was flying to mining zones. Most areas were cut off by road and rain and fog seriously hampered rescue operations by air, the prime minister said.

The latest of the 13 deaths to be confirmed included a young girl in Ica, 190 miles (305 km) south of Lima, a man, in Acari, 375 miles (600 km) south of the capital, and two men in the Leoncio Prado district of Ayacucho, 360 miles (575 km) south of Lima, Pedro Rivera.
Earlier officials had confirmed six people died in Nazca as well as one man in Ica, a woman in Acari and the miner in Moyohauca.
Nazca is one of Peru's main tourist attractions for its mysterious pre-Inca lines that form patterns in the desert that can be seen only from the air.

Nazca's museum about the lines was seriously damaged but "the lines are intact. They have put up with a lot of earthquakes over the years," said Ana-Maria Reiche, the adopted daughter of Maria Reiche, who dedicated her life to studying the lines.

Peru is prone to frequent seismic activity. On May 31, 1970, an earthquake measuring 7.8 in magnitude, killed 67,000 people as it leveled scores of towns in the district of Yungay, 240 miles (385 km) north of Lima, in the Ancash department.
